name: Southeast Glaciers (Standard)

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead
waypoints.note: Trailhead on SR 20 near milepost 134 (~14 mi east of Newhalem); Northwest Forest Pass needed for parking, trail drops steeply toward Ross Lake.
waypoints.directions: Reach the Ross Dam Trailhead at Happy Flats on SR-20 near milepost 134, about 14 miles east of Newhalem, at roughly 2,150 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park here.

waypoints.name: Ross Lake Put-in (foot of Ross Dam Trail)
waypoints.note: Trail bottoms out at the lakeshore, losing ~500 ft in 1.3 mi; meet the Ross Lake Resort water taxi (reserve in advance) or launch a packraft/canoe here for the crossing to Big Beaver.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Ross Dam Trail down through forest about a mile to the gravel service road and turn right toward the lake; turning left crosses the dam and adds a long detour. Before the shore, a post marked Resort Phone on the left leads to the phone box: call the resort and wait at the shuttle dock for the reserved water taxi, or launch a canoe or packraft here.

waypoints.name: Big Beaver Landing
waypoints.note: Water taxi/paddle drop-off roughly 4.6 mi up-lake from Ross Dam, at Ross Lake's full-pool elevation; start of the Big Beaver Creek Trail through ancient redcedar groves.
waypoints.directions: Ride the water taxi, or paddle, about 4.6 miles north up Ross Lake to Big Beaver Landing at the mouth of Big Beaver Creek on the west shore, where the Big Beaver Creek Trail begins.

waypoints.name: Luna Camp
waypoints.note: Established NPS backcountry campsite on Big Beaver Creek about 11.5 mi up the trail from the landing; last reliable flowing water and flat tentsites before leaving the maintained trail.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Big Beaver Creek Trail up the valley through groves of old-growth redcedar. The trail is well graded and largely flat, and Luna Camp, an established backcountry camp beside the creek, is reached after roughly 4 to 5 hours.

waypoints.name: Access Creek / Big Beaver Creek Ford
waypoints.note: About a mile past Luna Camp an unmaintained, orange-flagged climbers' path forks off and fords Big Beaver Creek through dense devil's club and alder; the crossing is unbridged and can run thigh-deep.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the Big Beaver Creek Trail about a mile, roughly half an hour, past Luna Camp, then leave the trail on the unmaintained, flagged climbers' path and cross Big Beaver Creek toward Access Creek. There is no bridge, so cross on a log or expect a cold ford that can run thigh-deep.

waypoints.name: Access Basin
waypoints.note: Steep, brushy mile-long climbers' path gains roughly 1,500 ft from the creek ford to a talus/heather basin at 4,300 ft, the standard high camp for the Access Creek approach.
waypoints.directions: Bushwhack up the Access Creek drainage for about a mile: devil's club in the valley bottom, a crossing to the creek's north side around 3,800 ft where the brush pinches in on both banks, then huckleberry brush and a final half-mile of talus into the basin at about 4,300 ft.

waypoints.name: Luna Pass (via Access Col)
waypoints.note: A steep scree chute gains Access Col at 6,100 ft, then notoriously steep heather and talus slopes lead to Luna Pass near 7,200 ft, the usual base camp for the summit push.
waypoints.directions: From the basin, climb the long, steep, loose scree chute about 1,800 ft to Access Col at 6,100 ft, which can be hot with no shade. From the col, traverse steep heather and talus to Luna Pass; an axe is worthwhile on the short steep heather sections.

waypoints.name: East Fury Summit
waypoints.note: Gained via a Northeast Ridge rock scramble around a knob (broad ledge traverse), a steep descending ramp to a snow saddle, then the Southeast Glacier (30-40°, steepening near 50° at the top); descend the same glacier's true right side.
waypoints.directions: Skirt the knob above Luna Pass on a broad ledge on its northwest side and follow the Northeast Ridge over its ups and downs, including a 25-ft Class 3 crack. Where the crest drops away, descend a narrow heather chute about 500 ft, contour southwest to a rocky rib and take its lower ledge, then rope up for the right side of the Southeast Glacier, passing a bergschrund near 7,900 ft and climbing snow to nearly 50 degrees to the summit.

approach: From the Ross Dam Trailhead at Happy Flats on SR 20 (~milepost 134, 2,150 ft), it's about 1 mile down to the Ross Lake water taxi dock; cross the lake by taxi (or paddle) to Big Beaver Landing. From the landing, follow the Big Beaver Creek Trail 11.5 miles up-valley — a dry, well-maintained, largely flat trail taking roughly 5 hours, passing Luna Camp around the 4.7-hour mark. About 29 minutes beyond Luna Camp, a large (~15-inch-diameter) log crossing of Big Beaver Creek marks the turnoff: leave the trail here and head up the Access Creek drainage. This next mile is a real bushwhack, gaining roughly 1,900 ft (2,400 ft to 4,300 ft): start in valley-bottom devil's club, cross to the creek's north side around 3,800 ft where brush pinches in on both banks, then climb through moderately dense huckleberry brush before the final half-mile of talus into Access Basin — watch for deadfall, thick undercover, and biting insects. From Access Basin, a long, steep, loose scree chute gains ~1,800 ft to 6,100-ft Access Col (2-3 hours; can be brutally hot with no shade in the chute). From the col, traverse 3-4 miles of notoriously steep heather (an axe is worthwhile for security on the short, steep sections) and talus to Luna Pass, where most parties camp near lingering snow patches for water. From Luna Pass, skirt a rock knob that towers ~100 ft over the pass via a broad ledge on its northwest face to reach the surprisingly gentle Northeast Ridge crest, then follow the ridge's many short ups and downs — including a ~25-ft rock step with a climbable vertical crack (Class 3) — toward Fury. Where the ridge crest drops away, descend a steep, narrow heather chute (~500 ft) into a talus basin around 6,500 ft, then contour southwest across talus, heather, and polished slabs to a rocky rib that blocks easy passage; the lower of two ledge options (exposed scrambling on wet, mossy rock and steep heather) is generally preferred to the looser, more exposed upper ledge.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake water taxi, Big Beaver Creek Trail, the Access Creek bushwhack, Access Col and Luna Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at Happy Flats on SR-20 near milepost 134 at 2,150 ft, walk about a mile down to the Ross Lake water-taxi dock and cross to Big Beaver Landing. From the landing, 11.5 miles of dry, well-maintained, largely flat trail up-valley takes roughly 5 hours, passing Luna Camp at about the 4.7-hour mark.

About 29 minutes beyond Luna Camp a large log crossing of Big Beaver Creek, roughly 15 inches in diameter, marks the turnoff. Leave the trail there and head up Access Creek: a real bushwhack of about a mile gaining 1,900 ft, starting in valley-bottom devil's club, crossing to the creek's north side around 3,800 ft where brush pinches in on both banks, then huckleberry and a final half-mile of talus into Access Basin.

From the basin a long, steep, loose scree chute gains about 1,800 ft to Access Col at 6,100 ft, 2-3 hours, and it can be brutally hot with no shade. From the col, 3-4 miles of notoriously steep heather and talus lead to Luna Pass, where most parties camp near lingering snow patches for water.
hazards: A mile of genuine bushwhacking up Access Creek through devil's club, deadfall and huckleberry with biting insects
A long loose scree chute to Access Col with no shade
Notoriously steep heather between Access Col and Luna Pass; an axe is worthwhile on the short steep sections
Crevasses on the Southeast Glacier and a bergschrund near 7,900 ft
A final snowfield to nearly 50 degrees, with crampon-balling reported on wet snow
Wet, mossy rock on the lower of the two rib ledges
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The rocky rib is the gate, and the glacier starts on the far side of it. From Luna Pass the day goes along the Northeast Ridge crest, then down a steep, narrow heather chute of about 500 ft into a talus basin around 6,500 ft, then contours southwest across talus, heather and polished slabs until a rocky rib blocks easy passage. That rib is the landmark. It has two ledge options: take the lower one, exposed scrambling on wet mossy rock and steep heather, in preference to the looser and more exposed upper ledge.

Arrival: immediately beyond the rib you rope up, because the Southeast Glacier starts there, between roughly 6,500 and 7,000 ft. Snow under your feet on the far side of the rib is the route.

Countable confirmation on the ridge: between Luna Pass and the heather chute the crest throws up one distinct rock step of about 25 ft with a climbable vertical crack, class 3. That step is the only rock climbing before the glacier. If you have done several such steps you are on the ridge crest too long and have missed the point where it drops away.

What being on the wrong side looks like: this route climbs the true right, i.e. climber's-right, side of the Southeast Glacier on moderate 20-40 degree snow and works around a bergschrund near 7,900 ft, usually passable on its left. If you are on the left-hand margin of the ice looking for a way onto rock, you are heading for the East Ridge, not this route.

And the one feature that is unmistakable even blind: the last of the route steepens from 30-40 degrees to nearly 50 degrees, firm enough to front-point but not always secure for flat-footing, then narrows to a short snow arete before the summit rocks. When the snow narrows to a crest with air on both sides, there is nothing above but the top.
